A **formal real polynomial** is either the zero polynomial $0$, or a finite coefficient list $(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$ with $a_n\ne0$; we write the latter as $p(X)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_kX^k$. The list, rather than the function it induces, is the polynomial object. Its **evaluation** at $x\in\mathbb R$ is the real number $p(x):=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_kx^k$.

For nonzero $p=(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$, define $\deg p:=n$ and $\operatorname{lc}(p):=a_n$. The zero polynomial has no degree and no leading coefficient. A nonzero polynomial is **monic** when $\operatorname{lc}(p)=1$. Thus degree and leading coefficient are defined from the displayed finite list, without asserting that distinct formal polynomials define distinct functions. The conventions for finite sums and integer powers used in the evaluation are recorded in [[def-finite-sum]], [[def-integer-power]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $f=\sum_{i\ge0}a_i x^i\in R[x]$. Its **formal derivative** is

$$ f':=\sum_{i\ge1} i a_i x^{i-1}. $$

Here $i a_i$ means the sum of $i$ copies of $a_i$ in the additive group of $R$. Equivalently, the coefficient of $x^n$ in $f'$ is $(n+1)a_{n+1}$. The sequence defining $f'$ has finite support because the coefficient sequence of $f$ does ([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]). This is an algebraic operation and does not use a limit.

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$ be the set of formal real polynomials of
[[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]]. Associate to every
$P\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$ an eventually zero coefficient sequence $(p_k)$:
use its displayed finite coefficient list and extend it by zeros when $P\ne0$,
and put $p_k=0$ for every $k$ when $P=0$. Do the same for $Q$, with coefficients
$(q_k)$. Define $P+Q$ coefficientwise and define $PQ$ by the convolution
coefficients
$$ (P+Q)_k=p_k+q_k,\qquad (PQ)_k=\sum_{j=0}^{k}p_jq_{k-j}. $$
using the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. In either construction, discard
trailing zero coefficients; if every coefficient is zero, the result is the zero
polynomial. Scalar multiplication and subtraction are the corresponding
coefficientwise operations. Thus these formulas define operations on the formal
coefficient-list objects, independently of evaluation.

Write $1=(1)$ and $X=(0,1)$, and define
$$ \Phi(P,Q):=(Q,2XQ-P)\qquad(P,Q\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}). $$
Apply [[thm-recursion]] to the set
$\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}\times\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$, first with initial value
$(1,X)$ and then with initial value $(1,2X)$, always using the function $\Phi$.
This gives unique pair sequences $H^T,H^U$. Define $T_n$ and $U_n$ to be the
first coordinates of $H^T_n$ and $H^U_n$, respectively. Since the first
coordinate of $\Phi(P,Q)$ is $Q$, the second coordinate of $H^T_n$ is
$T_{n+1}$ and the second coordinate of $H^U_n$ is $U_{n+1}$. Consequently
$$ T_0=1,\quad T_1=X,\quad T_{n+2}=2XT_{n+1}-T_n, $$
$$ U_0=1,\quad U_1=2X,\quad U_{n+2}=2XU_{n+1}-U_n $$
for every $n\in\mathbb N$. These unique sequences are the **Chebyshev
polynomials of the first and second kinds**.

For $n\ge1$, $T_n$ has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $2^{n-1}$, while $U_n$ has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $2^n$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]], [[thm-induction-principle]], [[def-integer-power]].

For every $n\in\mathbb N$ and real $\theta$,
$$T_n(\cos\theta)=\cos(n\theta),\qquad U_n(\cos\theta)\sin\theta=\sin((n+1)\theta).$$ In particular, for $n\ge1$ and $0\le j\le n$, $T_n(\cos(j\pi/n))=(-1)^j$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-induction-principle]].
$\sin\pi=0$, and $\sin x>0$ for every $x$ with $0<x<\pi$. Thus $\pi$ is the first positive zero of sine.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(\pi/2-x)=\cos x,\quad \cos(\pi/2-x)=\sin x,\quad \sin(\pi-x)=\sin x,\quad \cos(\pi-x)=-\cos x,$$
and the quarter-turn and reflection formulas are
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad \cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad \sin(-x)=-\sin x,\quad \cos(-x)=\cos x.$$
On the common natural domains of the two sides,
$$\tan(\pi/2-x)=\cot x,\quad \cot(\pi/2-x)=\tan x,\quad \sec(\pi/2-x)=\csc x,\quad \csc(\pi/2-x)=\sec x,$$
and
$$\tan(\pi-x)=-\tan x,\quad \cot(\pi-x)=-\cot x,\quad \sec(\pi-x)=-\sec x,\quad \csc(\pi-x)=\csc x.$$
The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

A nonzero real polynomial of degree $n$ has at most $n$ distinct real roots. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]], [[lem-real-polynomial-factor-at-a-root]], [[thm-induction-principle]].

If $p(x)=\sum_{k<n}a_kx^k$ and $p(a)=0$, then there is a real polynomial $q$ with $p(x)=(x-a)q(x)$ for every real $x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]], [[lem-power-difference-factorisation]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]].

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be **nonempty** and compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $\sup f[K]$ and $\inf f[K]$ exist and are
**attained**: there are $p, q \in K$ with

$$f(q) \;=\; \inf f[K] \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; \sup f[K] \;=\; f(p) \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, the set $f[K]$ has a maximum and a minimum
([[def-max-min]]), namely $\max f[K] = f(p)$ and $\min f[K] = f(q)$.

**Nonemptiness of $K$ is a hypothesis, not an oversight.** For $K = \varnothing$
the set $f[K]$ is empty, and neither a supremum nor a maximum of the empty set
exists in this library ([[def-complete-ordered-field]] supplies suprema of
nonempty sets bounded above only).

**This theorem is stated twice in this library, on purpose.** Its metric-space
twin is [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], proved from the cover machinery of metric
spaces; the proof below is $\mathbb{R}$-native, running through Heine-Borel for
$\mathbb{R}$ and the order-completeness of $\mathbb{R}$, and it uses no cover
argument beyond the one already spent in
[[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-set-r]]. That the two statements are the
same statement in two vocabularies is proved in
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]], later on this page.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

For every real $x$, $\sin ^2x+\cos ^2x=1$, $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$, and $\cos(-x)=\cos x$. Wherever the displayed quotients are defined, $\tan(-x)=-\tan x$, $\cot(-x)=-\cot x$, $\sec(-x)=\sec x$, $\csc(-x)=-\csc x$, $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$, and $1+\cot^2x=\csc^2x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $p$ and each polynomial $r$ below are finite real polynomials; [F2] and [F9] make $p,p'$ continuous and attain their extrema on $[-1,1]$. For any such $r$, $S_r(\theta):=\sin\theta\,r(\cos\theta)$ is continuous by [F6], [F9], and [F10], and is $2\pi$-periodic by [F15]; hence [F9] gives a maximum of $|S_r|$ on $[0,2\pi]$. If $d=0$ or $p=0$, then $p'=0$ and $h=0$; assume $d\ge1$. For $j=1,\ldots,d$, put $\theta_j=(2j-1)\pi/(2d)$ and $x_j=\cos\theta_j$. By [F4], $T_d(x_j)=\cos(d\theta_j)=0$. Monotonicity and reflection in [F5] show $x_1>\cdots>x_d$ in $(-1,1)$ and $x_d=-x_1$. Also [F5] gives $\sin\theta_j>0$. Since $d\theta_j=(j-1)\pi+\pi/2$, repeated use of the shift-by-$\pi$ identity in [F5], with finite induction [F13], gives $\sin(d\theta_j)=(-1)^{j-1}$. The chain rule [F6] applied to [F4] now gives $T_d'(x_j)=d\sin(d\theta_j)/\sin\theta_j=d(-1)^{j-1}/\sin\theta_j\ne0$.

Fix any polynomial $r$ supported in degrees at most $d-1$. For $x\in[-x_1,x_1]$, choose $\theta\in[0,\pi]$ with $x=\cos\theta$. Monotonicity and reflection in [F5] imply $\pi/(2d)\le\theta\le\pi-\pi/(2d)$, so $\sin\theta\ge\sin(\pi/(2d))$. For every positive integer $n$, $|\sin(n\phi)|\le n|\sin\phi|$: equality holds for $n=1$; the sine addition formula [F8] and $|\sin|,|\cos|\le1$ from [F5] give $|\sin((n+1)\phi)|\le|\sin(n\phi)|+|\sin\phi|$, so induction [F13] proves the claim. At $\phi=\pi/(2d)$ this yields $1=|\sin(d\phi)|\le d\sin\phi$, hence $\sin(\pi/(2d))\ge1/d$. Therefore $|r(x)|\le d|\sin\theta\,r(\cos\theta)|\le d\max_{\eta\in[0,2\pi]}|S_r(\eta)|$ throughout this central interval.

By the factor theorem [F7] and $T_d(x_j)=0$ from step 1.1, each quotient $T_d(X)/(X-x_j)$ is a polynomial of degree $d-1$, so the Lagrange polynomials $L_j(X):=T_d(X)/((X-x_j)T_d'(x_j))$ have degree at most $d-1$. At $x_i$ with $i
e j$, $L_j(x_i)=0$; at $x_j$, factorization $T_d(X)=(X-x_j)s_j(X)$ and product rule [F11] give $s_j(x_j)=T_d'(x_j)$, so $L_j(x_j)=1$. Thus every $r$ as in step 2.1 satisfies $r(X)=\sum_{j=1}^d r(x_j)L_j(X)$, since the difference has degree at most $d-1$ and $d$ distinct roots, hence vanishes by [F7]. Repeated factorization by [F7] gives $T_d(X)=c\prod_j(X-x_j)$ with $c
e0$ (degree $d$ by [F3]); repeated product rule gives $T_d'(X)=c\sum_j\prod_{k
e j}(X-x_k)$. Therefore the polynomial $\sum_j T_d(X)/(X-x_j)-T_d'(X)$ vanishes for every $X$ away from the nodes, an infinite set, so it is zero by the root bound [F7]. Substituting $1/T_d'(x_j)=(-1)^{j-1}\sin	heta_j/d$ from step 1.1 gives $r(X)= rac1d\sum_{j=1}^d(-1)^{j-1}\sin	heta_j\,r(x_j) rac{T_d(X)}{X-x_j}$.

Let $W:=\max_{\eta\in[0,2\pi]}|S_r(\eta)|$. At each node, $\sin\theta_j|r(x_j)|=|S_r(\theta_j)|\le W$. For $x\in(x_1,1]$, all $x-x_j>0$, and the interpolation formula of step 3.1 gives $|r(x)|\le(W/d)|T_d(x)|\sum_j1/(x-x_j)=(W/d)|T_d'(x)|$. For $x\in[-1,-x_1)$ all denominators are negative, so the summands $T_d(x)/(x-x_j)$ have a common sign and their absolute values sum to $|T_d'(x)|$; the same interpolation and node bounds give $|r(x)|\le(W/d)|T_d'(x)|$. For interior $x=\cos\theta$, $0<\theta<\pi$, differentiating [F4] by [F6] gives $|T_d'(x)|=d|\sin(d\theta)|/\sin\theta\le d^2$ by the sine estimate of step 2.1. Continuity extends this bound to the outer endpoints; the central boundary nodes are covered by step 2.1. Hence $|r(x)|\le dW$ on the outer intervals. Combining this with step 2.1 proves $\|r\|_{[-1,1]}\le d\max_{\eta\in[0,2\pi]}|S_r(\eta)|$ on all of $[-1,1]$.

For continuous $g$ on $[-1,1]$ write $\|g\|:=\max_{[-1,1]}|g|$; for continuous $2\pi$-periodic $S$ write $\|S\|_{\rm trig}:=\max_{[0,2\pi]}|S|$. Let $S$ be a real trigonometric polynomial of degree at most $d$, meaning a finite real linear combination of $1,\cos(k\theta),\sin(k\theta)$ for $1\le k\le d$. Its sine and cosine terms and their derivatives are continuous by [F6] and [F10], and are $2\pi$-periodic by [F15], so all maxima just defined, including that of $|S'|$, exist by [F9]. For fixed $\alpha$, $F_\alpha(\theta):=(S(\alpha+\theta)-S(\alpha-\theta))/2$ is a linear combination of $\sin(k\theta)$: the constant term cancels, each cosine term contributes $-\sin(k\alpha)\sin(k\theta)$, and each sine term contributes $\cos(k\alpha)\sin(k\theta)$ by the addition formulas [F8] and parity [F14]. By [F4], $\sin(k\theta)=\sin\theta\,U_{k-1}(\cos\theta)$, so $F_\alpha(\theta)=\sin\theta\,r(\cos\theta)$ for a polynomial $r$ supported in degrees at most $d-1$ by [F3]. By the chain rule [F6], differentiating the centered difference at $0$ gives $F_\alpha'(0)=(S'(\alpha)+S'(\alpha))/2=S'(\alpha)$. Differentiating the factorization using polynomial differentiability [F2], [F6], and [F11] gives $F_\alpha'(0)=r(1)$, because $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$ by [F6]. Thus $S'(\alpha)=r(1)$. By steps 2.1 and 4.1, $|r(1)|\le\|r\|\le d\|F_\alpha\|_{\rm trig}$. Also $\|F_\alpha\|_{\rm trig}\le\|S\|_{\rm trig}$ by [F12], since $F_\alpha$ is the half-difference of two values of $S$. As this holds for every $\alpha$, $\|S'\|_{\rm trig}\le d\|S\|_{\rm trig}$.

Put $S(\theta):=p(\cos\theta)$. Applying [F8] at $(u,v)$ and $(u,-v)$ and using [F14] gives $\cos u\cos v=(\cos(u+v)+\cos(u-v))/2$. Induction now gives that each power $\cos^k\theta$ is a linear combination of $\cos(j\theta)$ for $0\le j\le k$: multiplying a term $\cos(j\theta)$ by $\cos\theta$ gives frequencies $j+1$ and $j-1$ when $j\ge1$, while the constant term gives $\cos\theta$. Thus $S$ is a real trigonometric polynomial of degree at most $d$. Cosine decreases from $1$ to $-1$ on $[0,\pi]$ by [F5] and its endpoint values [F6], [F5], so its range on $[0,2\pi]$ is $[-1,1]$; with [F15] this gives $\|S\|_{\rm trig}=\|p\|$. The chain rule [F6] and polynomial differentiability [F2] give $S'(\theta)=-\sin\theta\,p'(\cos\theta)$, so step 5.1 gives $\max_{\theta\in[0,2\pi]}|\sin\theta\,p'(\cos\theta)|\le d\|p\|$. Applying the inequality proved in steps 2.1 and 4.1 to $r=p'$, whose degree is at most $d-1$ by [F2], yields $\|p'\|\le d\max_{\theta\in[0,2\pi]}|\sin\theta\,p'(\cos\theta)|\le d^2\|p\|$. The list, rather than the function it induces, is the polynomial object. Its **evaluation** at $x\in\mathbb R$ is the real number $p(x):=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_kx^k$.

For nonzero $p=(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$, define $\deg p:=n$ and $\operatorname{lc}(p):=a_n$. The zero polynomial has no degree and no leading coefficient. A nonzero polynomial is **monic** when $\operatorname{lc}(p)=1$. Thus degree and leading coefficient are defined from the displayed finite list, without asserting that distinct formal polynomials define distinct functions. The conventions for finite sums and integer powers used in the evaluation are recorded in [[def-finite-sum]], [[def-integer-power]].

   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for

A **local bit-query algorithm** is a finite rooted execution tree on one fixed finite ordered register, starting in the all-zero computational-basis state $|0^m\rangle$ for its fixed register length $m$. The tree topology and each node label are fixed independently of $x$. Each non-oracle node is either a fixed unitary or a fixed finite instrument, with its observed outcomes retained for later control; every such operation is independent of $x$. Each query node acts on a declared $N$-bit address register and a disjoint one-bit target register by the standard XOR oracle $U_{g_x}$ of [[def-qa-standard-bit-query]], tensored with the identity on all other wires. Every terminal node uses the same ordered output-wire tuple and the same fixed accepting subset $S\subseteq\{0,1\}^r$, independent of $x$; the output law sums over all unmeasured labels and all terminal branch histories as in [[def-qa-finite-branch-output-law]].

The **query count of a branch** is the number of query nodes on its root-to-terminal path. The algorithm makes at most $T$ queries when every such path contains at most $T$ query nodes. A local bit-query algorithm has **no direct input access**: there is no input register containing $x$, no $x$-dependent non-oracle operation or initial state, and no $x$-dependent terminal predicate. Thus $x$ enters only through the stated bit oracle. This is the oracle-only specialization used for the QA15 polynomial-method results.

Its root state is the density operator of the standard input basis state with zero-initialized work registers. Every nonterminal node is either a unitary endomorphism $U:H_n\to H_n$ or a finite instrument $(\mathcal I_a)_{a\in\Omega_h}$ whose branch maps are from $\mathcal L(H_n)$ to $\mathcal L(H_n)$. The observed outcome label $a$ is retained for classical feed-forward, while a hidden Kraus label is not a branch. The tree has finite depth and finite outcome sets.

factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

$$f=\sum_{\mathbf{t}}c_{\mathbf{t}}x^{\mathbf{t}},\qquad x^{\mathbf{t}}:=x_1^{t_1}\cdots x_n^{t_n},$$

$[x^{\mathbf{t}}]f$ of the monomial $x^{\mathbf{t}}$.

**total degree** is the largest value of $t_1+\cdots+t_n$ with
$c_{\mathbf{t}}\ne0$. For the zero polynomial, every degree is left undefined.

Evaluation at a point $(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in F^n$ is the iterated substitution
supplied by the universal property of the polynomial ring.

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of

$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

$$\sum_{a\in\Omega}\operatorname{tr}_K(\mathcal I_a(X))=\operatorname{tr}_H(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H).$$

derivations.claim: At the root, the branch weight is one and the state is the fixed all-zero basis-state projector, so every entry of $\sigma_\varnothing$ is constant and has no supported monomial above degree zero.

This support convention includes the zero polynomial at every $d\ge0$, although the formal zero polynomial has no degree ([[def-monomials-multidegree-and-total-degree]]).

Define $\bar p(x):=\frac1{N!}\sum_{\pi\in S_N}\widetilde p(x_{\pi(0)},\ldots,x_{\pi(N-1)})$. For $x\in D$, each permuted point is in $D$ and has $f(\pi x)=f(x)$, so [F1] gives $|\widetilde p(\pi x)-f(x)|\le\epsilon$ for every $\pi$. The triangle inequality for this finite average yields $|\bar p(x)-f(x)|\le\epsilon$.

Fix a set $S$ of size $s$. Under the average over $S_N$, each subset $R$ of size $s$ occurs as the permuted image of $S$ exactly $s!(N-s)!$ times. Hence the average of $X_S$ is $\binom Ns^{-1}\sum_{|R|=s}X_R$, a polynomial of degree at most $s$. Summing with coefficients $c_S$ shows that $\bar p$ has degree at most $d$ and is invariant under all coordinate permutations.

If $x$ has Hamming weight $t$, exactly $\binom ts$ of the squarefree monomials $x_R$ with $|R|=s$ equal $1$ (their index sets must lie inside the $t$ coordinates equal to $1$); all others equal $0$. Therefore the average of each degree-$s$ monomial at $x$ is $\binom ts/\binom Ns=(t)_s/(N)_s$, where $(t)_s=t(t-1)\cdots(t-s+1)$ and $(t)_0=1$. The denominator $(N)_s$ is nonzero for $s\le N$ by [F4]. Thus $\bar p(x)=q(|x|)$ for the univariate polynomial $q(t)=\sum_S c_S(t)_{|S|}/(N)_{|S|}$, with the $s=0$ term interpreted as $1$. Each summand has degree $|S|\le d$, so $\deg q\le d$. By step 2.1 it retains the approximation bound on $D$.

If $N=0$, the address set has only the empty word and $g_x$ is identically zero. A **local bit-query algorithm** is a finite rooted execution tree on one fixed finite ordered register, starting in the all-zero computational-basis state $|0^m\rangle$ for its fixed register length $m$. The tree topology and each node label are fixed independently of $x$. Each non-oracle node is either a fixed unitary or a fixed finite instrument, with its observed outcomes retained for later control; every such operation is independent of $x$. Each query node acts on a declared $N$-bit address register and a disjoint one-bit target register by the standard XOR oracle $U_{g_x}$ of [[def-qa-standard-bit-query]], tensored with the identity on all other wires. Every terminal node uses the same ordered output-wire tuple and the same fixed accepting subset $S\subseteq\{0,1\}^r$, independent of $x$; the output law sums over all unmeasured labels and all terminal branch histories as in [[def-qa-finite-branch-output-law]].

The **query count of a branch** is the number of query nodes on its root-to-terminal path. The algorithm makes at most $T$ queries when every such path contains at most $T$ query nodes. A local bit-query algorithm has **no direct input access**: there is no input register containing $x$, no $x$-dependent non-oracle operation or initial state, and no $x$-dependent terminal predicate. Thus $x$ enters only through the stated bit oracle. This is the oracle-only specialization used for the QA15 polynomial-method results.

derivations.claim: The matrices in [F3] and [F4] satisfy $H^*H=I$ and $X^*X=I$ by direct multiplication; the CNOT action in [F3] permutes the four computational-basis vectors, so it is unitary. Starting at $|00,0\rangle$, apply $X$ to the second address bit, then $H$ to the first and CNOT from the first to the second. The basis actions in [F3]–[F4] give $\frac1{\sqrt2}(|01,0\rangle+|10,0\rangle)=\frac1{\sqrt2}(|e_1,0\rangle+|e_0,0\rangle)$. These are fixed input-independent unitaries permitted by [F1].

One oracle call and [F2] transform this to $\frac1{\sqrt2}(|e_1,x_1\rangle+|e_0,x_0\rangle)$. Measuring the target and accepting exactly when it is $1$ has probability $\frac12|x_1|^2+\frac12|x_0|^2=(x_0+x_1)/2$, because the orthogonal address basis states have no cross terms and each $x_i$ is a bit. This gives the stated acceptance polynomial.

On $00$ the acceptance probability is $0=f(00)$, and on $11$ it is $1=f(11)$, so the algorithm is exact on $D$ with one query. The polynomial $p$ has total degree one by [F7]. Thus $\widetilde{\deg}_0(f;D)=1$ by [F5], and the one-query construction verifies $Q^{\mathrm{bit}}_0(f;D)\le1$ by [F6].
